title: De Divinatione
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
source: Translated by Claude from phi0474.phi053.perseus-lat4, as held by the Perseus Digital Library.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit the Perseus Digital Library and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: magnifica quaedam res et salutaris, si modo est ulla, quaque proxime ad deorum vim natura mortalis possit accedere. itaque ut alia nos melius multa quam Graeci, sic huic praestantissimae rei nomen nostri a divis, Graeci, ut Plato interpretatur, a furore duxerunt.
passages.english: [It is] a splendid and salutary thing, if only it exists at all, and one by which mortal nature might come closest to the power of the gods. And so, just as we [Romans] have done many other things better than the Greeks, so our people took the name of this most excellent thing from the gods (divi), while the Greeks, as Plato interprets it, took theirs from madness (furor).
passages.notes: Cicero alludes to the derivation of Latin divinatio from divi 'gods' and Greek mantikē from mania 'madness'.

passages.original: An medicine ars non putanda est? quam tamen multa fallunt. quid? gubernatores nonne falluntur? An Achivorum exercitus et tot navium rectores non ita profecti sunt ab Ilio, ut profectione laeti piscium lasciviam intuerentur, ut ait Pacuvius, nec tuendi satietas capere posset?interea prope iam óccidente sóle inhorrescít mare,ténebrae conduplicántur noctisque ét nimbum occaecát nigror. Num igitur tot clarissimorum ducum regumque naufragium sustulit artem gubernandi?
passages.english: Is medicine not to be considered an art? Yet many things deceive it. What then? Are pilots not deceived? Did not the army of the Achaeans and the captains of so many ships set out from Ilium in such a way that, glad at their departure, they watched the playfulness of the fish, as Pacuvius says, and could not have their fill of gazing? "Meanwhile, with the sun now almost setting, the sea grows rough, the darkness doubles, and the blackness of night and cloud blinds [them]." Did the shipwreck of so many most illustrious leaders and kings, then, abolish the art of piloting?

passages.original: carent autem arte ei qui, non ratione aut coniectura observatis ac notatis signis, sed concitatione quadam animi aut soluto liberoque motu, futura praesentiunt, quod et somniantibus saepe contingit et non numquam vaticinantibus per furorem, ut Bacis Boeotius, ut Epimenides Cres, ut Sibylla Erythraea. cuius generis oracula etiam habenda sunt, non ea, quae aequatis sortibus ducuntur, sed illa, quae instinctu divino afflatuque funduntur; etsi ipsa sors contemnenda non est, si auctoritatem habet vetustatis, ut eae sunt sortes, quas e terra editas accepimus;
passages.english: But those lack art who foresee future things not by reason or conjecture from signs observed and noted, but by a certain excitement of the mind or by a free and unfettered movement [of it]. This often happens to people dreaming, and sometimes to those who prophesy through frenzy, like Bacis of Boeotia, like Epimenides of Crete, like the Erythraean Sibyl. To this class must also be assigned oracles, not those drawn by evenly shaken lots, but those poured forth by divine impulse and inspiration; although the lot itself is not to be despised, if it has the authority of antiquity, as do those lots which, we are told, were brought forth from the earth;

passages.original: Num te ad fabulas revoco vel nostrorum vel Graecorum poëtarum? narrat enim et apud Ennium Vestalis illa: excita cum tremulis anus attulit artubu’ lumen,talia tum memorat lacrimans exterrita somno:Eurydica prognata, pater quam noster amavit,vires vitaque corpu’ meum nunc deserit omne.nam me visus homo pulcher per amoena salicta et ripas raptare locosque novos;
passages.english: Am I calling you back to the tales of the poets, either ours or the Greeks'? For in Ennius too that Vestal relates: "When the old woman, roused, had brought a light with trembling limbs, then, weeping and terrified from sleep, she tells such things: 'Daughter of Eurydice, whom our father loved, strength and life now leave my whole body. For a handsome man seemed to carry me off through pleasant willow groves and banks and unfamiliar places;'"
passages.notes: The 'Vestal' is Ilia, mother of Romulus and Remus; the speech is addressed to her sister.

passages.original: Sed propiora videamus. cuiusnam modi est Superbi Tarquini somnium, de quo in Bruto Acci loquitur ipse?
passages.english: But let us look at things nearer [to us]. Of what kind is the dream of Tarquin the Proud, about which he himself speaks in Accius' Brutus?

passages.original: Est apud Platonem Socrates, cum esset in custodia publica, dicens Critoni, suo familiari, sibi post tertium diem esse moriendum; vidisse enim se in somnis pulchritudine eximia feminam, quae se nomine appellans, diceret Homericum quendam eius modi versum: tertia te Phthiae tempestas laeta locabit.quod, ut est dictum, sic scribitur contigisse.
passages.english: In Plato there is Socrates, when he was in the public prison, telling Crito, his friend, that he must die after the third day; for he had seen in his sleep a woman of exceptional beauty who, calling him by name, spoke a certain Homeric verse of this kind: "The third fair day will set you in Phthia." And it is written that this happened just as it had been said.

passages.original: ei visum in quiete egregia facie iuvenem dicere fore ut perbrevi convalesceret, paucisque diebus interiturum Alexandrum tyrannum, ipsum autem Eudemum quinquennio post domum esse rediturum. atque ita quidem prima statim scribit Aristoteles consecuta, et convaluisse Eudemum, et ab uxoris fratribus interfectum tyrannum; quinto autem anno exeunte, cum esset spes ex illo somnio in Cyprum ilium ex Sicilia esse rediturum, proeliantem eum ad Syracusas occidisse;
passages.english: [that] in his sleep a young man of outstanding appearance seemed to tell him that he would very soon recover, that the tyrant Alexander would perish within a few days, and that Eudemus himself would return home five years later. And Aristotle writes that the first [predictions] were fulfilled at once: Eudemus recovered, and the tyrant was killed by his wife's brothers; but at the end of the fifth year, when there was hope from that dream that he would return from Sicily to Cyprus, he fell fighting at Syracuse;

passages.original: Marium cum fascibus laureatis quaerere ex te, quid tristis esses, cumque tu te patria vi pulsum esse dixisses, prehendisse eum dextram tuam et bono animo te iussisse esse lictorique proximo tradidisse, ut te in monumentum suum deduceret, et dixisse in eo tibi salutem fore. tum et se exclamasse Sallustius narrat reditum tibi celerem et gloriosum paratum, et te ipsum visum somnio delectari. nam illud mihi ipsi celeriter nuntiatum est ut audivisses in monumento Mari de tuo reditu magnificentissimum illud senatus consultum esse factum referente optimo et clarissimo viro consule, idque frequentissimo theatro incredibili clamore et plausu comprobatum, dixisse te nihil illo Atinati somnio fieri posse divinius.
passages.english: [it seemed to you that] Gaius Marius, with his fasces wreathed in laurel, asked you why you were sad, and when you had said you had been driven from your country by force, he took your right hand, told you to be of good heart, and handed you over to the nearest lictor to escort you to his monument, and said that there your safety would lie. Then, Sallustius relates, he himself cried out that a swift and glorious return had been prepared for you, and you yourself seemed delighted by the dream. For this was quickly reported to me myself: that when you heard that it was in the monument of Marius that that most splendid decree of the senate about your return had been passed, on the motion of a most excellent and distinguished man, the consul, and that it had been approved in a packed theatre with incredible shouting and applause, you said that nothing could be more divinely inspired than that dream at Atina.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence, continuing the indirect speech of the dream from the preceding context ('C.' = Gaius). Sallustius here is Cicero's companion, not the historian.

passages.original: Divinare autem morientes illo etiam exemplo confirmat Posidonius, quod affert, Rhodium quendam morientem sex aequales nominasse et dixisse, qui primus eorum, qui secundus, qui deinde deinceps moriturus esset. sed tribus modis censet deorum appulsu homines somniare: uno, quod praevideat animus ipse per sese, quippe qui deorum cognatione teneatur;
passages.english: Posidonius also confirms that the dying divine by this example, which he cites: that a certain Rhodian, when dying, named six men of his own age and said which of them would die first, which second, and which next in turn. But he holds that men dream by the impulse of the gods in three ways: in one, because the mind foresees by itself, inasmuch as it is bound by kinship with the gods;

passages.original: quorum alia sunt posita in monumentis et disciplina, quod Etruscorum declarant et haruspicini et fulgurales et tonitruales libri, vestri etiam augurales; alia autem subito ex tempore coniectura explicantur, ut apud Homerum Calchas, qui ex passerum numero belli Troiani annos auguratus est; et ut in Sullae scriptum historia videmus, quod te inspectante factum est, ut, cum ille in agro Nolano immolaret ante praetorium, ab infima ara subito anguis emergeret, cum quidem C.
passages.english: Of these, some are set down in records and in a body of teaching, as is shown by the Etruscan books on haruspicy, on lightning, and on thunder, and also by your augural books; others are explained on the spot by sudden conjecture, as Calchas in Homer, who foretold the years of the Trojan War from the number of sparrows; and as we see written in Sulla's history, something that happened while you were watching: when he was sacrificing in the territory of Nola in front of his headquarters, a snake suddenly emerged from the bottom of the altar, at which point Gaius
passages.notes: The sentence breaks off at the praenomen 'C.'; the name Postumius follows in the next passage.

passages.original: Atque etiam illa concitatio declarat vim in animis esse divinam. negat enim sine furore Democritus quemquam poëtam magnum esse posse, quod idem dicit Plato. quem, si placet, appellet furorem, dum modo is furor ita laudetur, ut in Phaedro Platonis laudatus est. quid? vestra oratio in causis, quid ipsa actio potest esse vehemens et gravis et copiosa, nisi est animus ipse commotior?
passages.english: And that excitement too shows that there is a divine power in minds. For Democritus denies that anyone can be a great poet without madness, and Plato says the same. Let him call it madness, if he likes, provided that this madness is praised as it was praised in Plato's Phaedrus. What of it? Your oratory in court cases, your very delivery: how can it be vehement, weighty and copious unless the mind itself is more than usually stirred?

passages.original: Quis est autem quem non moveat clarissimis monumentis testata consignataque antiquitas? Calchantem augurem scribit Homerus longe optimum, eumque ducem classium fuisse ad Ilium, auspiciorum credo scientia, non locorum.
passages.english: And who is there who is not moved by antiquity, attested and sealed by the most illustrious records? Homer writes that Calchas was by far the best augur, and that he was the leader of the fleets to Ilium, by his knowledge of auspices, I suppose, not of places.

passages.original: amphilochus et Mopsus Argivorum reges fuerunt, sed eidem augures, eique urbis in ora maritima Ciliciae Graecas condiderunt; atque etiam ante hos Amphiaraus et Tiresias non humiles et obscuri neque eorum similes, ut apud Ennium est, quí sui quaestus caúsa fictas súscitant senténtias. sed clari et praestantes viri, qui avibus et signis admoniti futura dicebant; quorum de altero etiam apud inferos Homerus ait solum sapere, ceteros umbrarum vagari modo; Amphiaraum autem sic honoravit fama Graeciae, deus ut haberetur, atque ut ab eius solo, in quo est humatus, oracla peterentur.
passages.english: Amphilochus and Mopsus were kings of the Argives, but they were also augurs, and they founded Greek cities on the coast of Cilicia; and even before them Amphiaraus and Tiresias were not lowly and obscure men, nor like those who, as in Ennius, "stir up invented pronouncements for the sake of their own profit," but famous and outstanding men, who, warned by birds and signs, foretold the future. Of one of them Homer says that even among the dead he alone is wise, while the rest wander like shadows; Amphiaraus, moreover, the renown of Greece so honoured that he was held to be a god, and oracles were sought from the ground in which he was buried.
passages.notes: 'Of one of them' refers to Tiresias.

passages.original: Atque ille Romuli auguratus pastoralis, non urbanus fuit, nec fictus ad opiniones inperitorum, sed a certis acceptus et posteris traditus. itaque Romulus augur, ut apud Ennium est, cum fratre item augure curantes magna cum cura tum concupientes regni dant operam simul auspicio augurioque.hinc Remus auspicio se devovet atque secundam solus avem servat. at Romulus pulcher in alto quaerit Aventino, servat genus altivolantum.certabant, urbem Romam Remoramne vocarent.omnibus cura viris, uter esset induperator.exspectant;
passages.english: And that augury of Romulus was pastoral, not of the city, nor invented to suit the opinions of the ignorant, but received from reliable [sources] and handed down to posterity. Thus Romulus the augur, as in Ennius, with his brother, likewise an augur: "Then, taking care with great care, desiring the kingship, they apply themselves together to auspice and augury. Here Remus devotes himself to the auspice and watches alone for a favourable bird; but handsome Romulus seeks on the lofty Aventine, watches for the high-flying kind. They were contending whether to call the city Roma or Remora. All men were anxious which of the two would be ruler. They wait;"
passages.notes: 'secundam avem' may mean 'favourable bird'. The Ennius text has a known inconsistency about which hill Remus watched from.

passages.original: Eiusdem generis etiam illud est, quod scribit Herodotus, Croesi filium, cum esset infans, locutum; quo ostento regnum patris et domum funditus concidisse. caput arsisse Servio Tullio dormienti quae historia non prodidit? ut igitur, qui se tradit quieti praeparato animo cum bonis cogitationibus, tum rebus ad tranquillitatem accommodatis, certa et vera cernit in somnis;
passages.english: Of the same kind too is the story Herodotus writes, that the son of Croesus spoke when he was an infant; and that by this portent his father's kingdom and house utterly collapsed. What history has not recorded that Servius Tullius' head blazed while he slept? So, just as one who gives himself to rest with a mind prepared both by good thoughts and by circumstances suited to tranquillity sees certain and true things in his dreams;

passages.original: Scriptum est item, cum Critonis, sui familiaris, oculum alligatum vidisset, quaesivisse, quid esset; cum autem ille respondisset in agro, ambulanti ramulum adductum, ut remissus esset, in oculum suum recidisse, tum Socrates: Non enim paruisti mihi revocanti, cum uterer, qua soleo, praesagitione divina. Idem etiam Socrates, cum apud Delium male pugnatum esset Lachete praetore fugeretque cum ipso Lachete, ut ventum est in trivium, eadem, qua ceteri, fugere noluit.
passages.english: It is likewise written that when [Socrates] saw the eye of Crito, his friend, bandaged, he asked what it was; and when Crito answered that while he was walking in the country a branch pulled aside had sprung back, when released, into his eye, Socrates then said: "That is because you did not obey me when I called you back, since I was using the divine presentiment I usually use." The same Socrates, too, when the battle at Delium had gone badly under the command of Laches and he was fleeing with Laches himself, refused, when they came to a place where three roads met, to flee by the same road as the rest.

passages.original: Quocirca primum mihi videtur, ut Posidonius facit, a deo, de quo satis dictum est, deinde a fato, deinde a natura, vis omnis divinandi ratioque repetenda. fieri igitur omnia fato ratio cogit fateri. fatum autem id appello, quod Graeci edJuap/evrv, id est ordinem seriemque causarum, cum causae causa nexa rem ex se gignat.
passages.english: Therefore it seems to me that, as Posidonius does, the whole power and principle of divination should be traced first from god, about whom enough has been said, then from fate, then from nature. Reason compels us to admit that all things happen by fate. Now I call fate what the Greeks call heimarmenē, that is, an order and series of causes, when cause linked to cause produces a thing from itself.
passages.notes: The Greek word is garbled by scanning (edJuap/evrv); read εἱμαρμένην (heimarmenē).

passages.original: Democritus autem censet sapienter instituisse veteres, ut hostiarum immolatarum inspicerentur exta; quorum ex habitu atque ex colore tum salubritatis, tum pestilentiae signa percipi, non numquam etiam, quae sit vel sterilitas agrorum vel fertilitas futura.
passages.english: Democritus, moreover, holds that the ancients wisely established that the entrails of sacrificed victims should be inspected; [for] from their condition and colour signs are perceived, now of healthiness, now of pestilence, and sometimes too of what the barrenness or fertility of the fields will be.

passages.original: Addunt ad extremum, omnia levius casura rebus divinis procuratis. Si autem nihil fit extra fatum, nihil levari re divina potest. hoc sentit Homerus cum querentem Iovem inducit quod Sarpedonem filium a morte contra fatum eripere non posset. hoc idem significat Graecus ille in eam sententiam versus: quod fóre paratum est, ìd summum exsuperát Iovem.totum omnino fatum etiam Atellanio versu iure mihi esse irrisum videtur;

sed tamen eo concesso qui evenit, ut is, qui impetrire velit, convenientem hostiam rebus suis immolet? hoc erat, quod ego non rebar posse dissolvi. At quam festive dissolvitur! pudet me non tui quidem, cuius etiam memoriam admiror, sed Chrysippi, Antipatri, Posidonii, qui idem istuc quidem dicunt, quod est dictum a te, ad hostiam deligendam ducem esse vim quandam sentientem atque divinam, quae toto confusa mundo sit.
passages.english: But even granting that, how does it come about that the one who wishes to obtain a favourable omen sacrifices a victim suited to his affairs? This was what I thought could not be resolved. But how wittily it is resolved! I am ashamed, not of you indeed, whose memory I even admire, but of Chrysippus, Antipater, and Posidonius, who say exactly what was said by you: that the guide in choosing the victim is a certain sentient and divine power, which is diffused through the whole universe.
passages.notes: 'impetrire' is a rare augural verb, 'to obtain a good omen'.

passages.original: Democritus quidem optimis verbis causam explicat cur ante lucem galli canant; depulso enim de pectore et in omne corpus diviso et mitificato cibo cantus edere quiete satiatos; qui quidem silentio noctis, ut ait Ennius, favent faucíbus russis cantu plausuque prem’int alas.cum igitur hoc animal tam sit canorum sua sponte, quid in mentem venit Callistheni dicere deos gallis signum dedisse cantandi, cum id vel natura vel casus efficere potuisset?
passages.english: Democritus indeed explains in excellent words the reason why cocks crow before daylight: for when the food has been driven down from the chest and distributed through the whole body and softened, they utter their songs, sated with rest; and these, as Ennius says, in the silence of the night "indulge their ruddy throats with song and beat their wings with clapping." Since, then, this creature is so given to song of its own accord, what came into Callisthenes' head to say that the gods had given cocks a signal to crow, when either nature or chance could have brought this about?
passages.notes: Text contains scanning errors ("faucíbus", "prem’int"); read as "faucibus" and "premunt". The Ennius quotation is verse, here run into the prose.

passages.original: Nam illud mirarer—si crederem—quod apud Homerum Calchantem dixisti ex passerum numero belli Troiani annos auguratum; de cuius coniectura sic apud Homerum, ut nos otiosi convertimus, loquitur Agamemnon: ferte, viri, et duros animo tolerate labores,auguris ut nostri Calchantis fata queamus scire ratosne habeant an vanos pectoris orsus.namque omnes memori portentum mente retentant,qui non funestis liquerunt lumina fatis.argolicis primum ut vestita est classibus Aulis,quae Priamo cladem et Troiae pestemque ferebant, nos circum latices gelidos fumantibus aris,aurigeris divom placantes numina tauris,sub platano umbrifera, fons unde emanat aquai,vidimus immani specie tortuque draconem terribilem, Iovis ut pulsu penetrabat ab ara;qui platani in ramo foliorum tegmine saeptos corripuit pullos;
passages.english:
For I would marvel at this, if I believed it, which you said: that Calchas in Homer foretold the years of the Trojan War from the number of sparrows. About his conjecture Agamemnon speaks thus in Homer, as I translated it in my leisure:
Bear up, men, and endure hard toils in your spirit,
so that we may learn whether the prophecies of our augur Calchas
hold the counsels of his heart fixed or vain.
For all keep the portent in mindful memory
who have not left the light by deadly fate.
When Aulis was first clothed with the Argive fleets,
which were bearing slaughter to Priam and ruin to Troy,
we, around the cool springs, at smoking altars,
appeasing the divine powers of the gods with gold-horned bulls,
under a shady plane tree, from where a spring of water flows,
saw a serpent of monstrous form and coils,
terrible, as it came forth from the altar at Jupiter's impulse;
it seized the chicks hidden by the covering of leaves
on a branch of the plane tree;

passages.original: quae autem est inter augures conveniens et coniuncta constantia? ad nostri auguri consuetudinem dixit Ennius: tum tonuit laevum bene tempestate serena.
passages.english: And what consistent and coherent agreement is there among augurs? Following the custom of our augury, Ennius said: "Then it thundered on the left, favourably, in clear weather."
passages.notes: "bene" may be construed with "tonuit" (thundered favourably) or with "serena" (in quite clear weather).

passages.original: illudne dubium est, quin multi, cum ita nati essent, ut quaedam contra naturam depravata haberent, restituerentur et corrigerentur ab natura, cum se ipsa revocasset, aut arte atque medicina? ut, quorum linguae sic inhaererent, ut loqui non possent, eae scalpello resectae liberarentur. multi etiam naturae vitium meditatione atque exercitatione sustulerunt, ut Demosthenem scribit Phalereus, cum rho dicere nequiret, exercitatione fecisse, ut planissime diceret. quodsi haec astro ingenerata et tradita essent, nulla res ea mutare posset. quid? dissimilitudo locorum nonne dissimilis hominum procreationes habet?
passages.english: Is there any doubt that many people, though they had been born with certain parts deformed against nature, were restored and corrected by nature, when she had recovered herself, or by art and medicine? For example, those whose tongues were so tied that they could not speak had them freed by being cut loose with a scalpel. Many also have removed a natural defect by study and practice, as Phalereus writes of Demosthenes: that though he could not say *rho*, by practice he brought it about that he pronounced it most clearly. But if these things had been implanted and handed down by a star, nothing could change them. What then? Does not the difference of places produce different kinds of human offspring?
passages.notes: Phalereus: Demetrius of Phalerum. The last sentence is a question; the plural 'procreationes' is rendered as 'kinds of offspring'.

passages.original: quis enim est qui credat Apollinis ex oraculo Pyrrho esse responsum: aio te, Aeacida, Romanos vincere posse?primum Latine Apollo numquam locutus est; deinde ista sors inaudita Graecis est; praeterea Pyrrhi temporibus iam Apollo versus facere desierat; postremo, quamquam semper fuit, ut apud Ennium est, stolidum genus Aeacidarum,bellipotentes sunt magis quam sapientipotentes, tamen hanc amphiboliam versus intellegere potuisset, vincere te Romanos nihilo magis in se quam in Romanos valere; nam illa amphibolia quae Croesum decepit, vel Chrysippum potuisset fallere, haec vero ne Epicurum quidem!
passages.english: For who is there who would believe that this response was given to Pyrrhus from the oracle of Apollo: "I say that you, son of Aeacus, the Romans can conquer"? First, Apollo never spoke Latin; next, that oracle is unheard of among the Greeks; moreover, by Pyrrhus' time Apollo had already stopped composing verses; finally, although, as it is in Ennius, "the race of the Aeacidae was always dull-witted, mighty in war rather than mighty in wisdom," still he could have understood the ambiguity of this verse, that "you the Romans to conquer" applied no more against himself than against the Romans. For that ambiguity which deceived Croesus could have misled even Chrysippus, but this one not even Epicurus!
passages.notes: The oracle's Latin "aio te, Aeacida, Romanos vincere posse" is deliberately ambiguous (either you can conquer the Romans, or the Romans can conquer you); the English keeps the word order to preserve it.

passages.original: Utrum igitur censemus dormientium animos per sene ipsos in somniando moveri, an, ut Democritus censet, externa et adventicia visione pulsari? sive enim sic est sive illo modo, videri possunt permulta somniantibus falsa pro veris. nam et navigantibus moveri videntur ea quae stant, et quodam obtutu oculorum duo pro uno lucernae lumina.
passages.english: Do we think, then, that the minds of sleepers are moved of themselves in dreaming, or, as Democritus thinks, struck by an external, incoming vision? For whether it is this way or that, a great many false things can appear true to dreamers. For to people sailing, things that are standing still seem to move, and with a certain way of fixing the eyes, two lamp-flames seem to appear instead of one.
passages.notes: 'per sene ipsos' is read as 'per se ipsos' (scanning or text error).

passages.original: Iam vero quis dicere audeat vera omnia esse somnia? Aliquot somnia vera, inquit Ennius, sed omnia non est necesse. Quae est tandem ista distinctio? quae vera, quae falsa habet? et, si vera a deo mittuntur, falsa unde nascuntur? nam si ea quoque divina quid inconstantius deo? quid inscitius autem est quam mentes mortalium falsis et mendacibus visis concitare?
passages.english: Now who would dare to say that all dreams are true? "Some dreams are true," says Ennius, "but it is not necessary that all are." What, pray, is that distinction? What does it count as true, what as false? And if the true ones are sent by a god, where do the false ones arise from? For if those too are divine, what is more inconstant than a god? And what is more ignorant than to stir up the minds of mortals with false and lying visions?

passages.original: naturam autem eam dico, qua numquam animus insistens agitatione et motu esse vacuus potest. is cum languore corporis nec membris uti nec sensibus potest, incidit in visa varia et incerta ex reliquiis, ut ait Aristoteles, inhaerentibus earum rerum, quas vigilans gesserit aut cogitaverit. Quarum perturbatione mirabiles interdum existunt species somniorum; quae si alia falsa, alia vera, qua nota internoscantur, scire sane velim.
passages.english: And I call that its nature by which the mind, never resting, can never be free of agitation and motion. When, because of the body's weariness, it can use neither limbs nor senses, it falls into varied and uncertain visions arising, as Aristotle says, from the remnants that cling to it of the things it did or thought while awake. From the disturbance of these, marvellous forms of dreams sometimes arise; and if some of them are false and others true, I should very much like to know by what mark they are distinguished.

passages.original: Chrysippus quidem divinationem definit his verbis: vim cognoscentem et videntem et explicantem signa, quae a dis hominibus portendantur; officium autem esse eius praenoscere, dei erga homines mente qua sint quidque significent, quem ad modumque ea procurentur atque expientur. Idemque somniorum coniectionem definit hoc modo: esse vim cernentem et explanantem, quae a dis hominibus significentur in somnis. Quid ergo? ad haec mediocri opus est prudentia an et ingenio praestanti et eruditione perfecta?
passages.english: Chrysippus, indeed, defines divination in these words: a power that recognizes, sees and explains the signs that are foretold to men by the gods; and its function, he says, is to know in advance with what disposition the gods are toward men, what they signify, and how these [signs] are to be averted and expiated. And he likewise defines the interpretation of dreams in this way: that it is a power that discerns and explains what is signified to men by the gods in dreams. What then? For these things is moderate good sense needed, or both outstanding talent and complete learning?

passages.original: quam multi inopes digni praesidio deorum nullo somnio ad thesaurum reperiendum admonentur! quam autem ob causam tam est obscure admonitus ut ex ovo nasceretur thesauri similitudo, potius quam aperte thesaurum quaerere iuberetur, sicut aperte Simonides vetitus est navigare?
passages.english: How many poor people, worthy of the gods' help, are prompted by no dream to find treasure! And for what reason was he prompted so obscurely that a likeness of treasure arose from an egg, rather than being told openly to look for treasure, just as Simonides was openly forbidden to sail?

passages.original: quem enim tu Marium visum a me putas? Speciem, credo, eius et imaginem, ut Democrito videtur. unde profectam imaginem? A corporibus enim solidis et a certis figuris vult fluere imagines. Quod igitur Marii corpus erat? Ex eo, inquit, quod fuerat. Ista igitur me imago Mari in campum Atinatem persequebatur?
passages.english: For what Marius do you suppose I saw? His appearance, I suppose, and image, as Democritus holds. Where did the image come from? For he would have it that images flow from solid bodies and from definite shapes. What body of Marius, then, was there? 'From that which there had been,' he says. So that image of Marius was following me onto the plain of Atina?
